subject: Career
title: The Peter Principle
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Peter Principle.

hook.text: The best salesperson gets promoted to sales manager. She's terrible at managing. But she was great at selling.

buildup.text: Laurence Peter proposed: people rise to their level of incompetence. Promoted for success, stuck at failure.

discovery.text: Each promotion requires a new skill set. Excellence in role A doesn't guarantee competence in role B.

twist.text: A 2018 study of 53,000 sales workers confirmed it: the best salespeople made the worst managers.

climax.text: Smart organizations promote based on competence for the next role, not performance in the current one.

punchline.text: Being great at your job doesn't mean the next job is right for you.

quiz.question: What does the Peter Principle state?
options: People rise to their level of incompetence
Hard work always leads to promotion
Managers are always the best workers

details.summary: Laurence Peter's principle states that employees are promoted based on performance in their current role until they reach a level where they are no longer competent. The result is organizations filled with people performing above their ability level.
details.whyItMatters: The Peter Principle explains widespread management dysfunction. Recognizing it helps you avoid accepting promotions that move you away from your strengths.
takeaways: Promotion criteria rarely match the skills needed at the next level
Great individual contributors do not automatically make great managers
Lateral moves that match your strengths may beat upward promotions

faq.question: How can organizations avoid the Peter Principle in their promotion practices?
faq.answer: Promote based on demonstrated competency for the next role rather than performance in the current one. Provide training before promotion, create dual career tracks for individual contributors, and allow people to step back without stigma if the new role is a poor fit.

faq.question: Should you ever turn down a promotion to avoid the Peter Principle?
faq.answer: Yes, if the promotion moves you into a role that does not match your strengths or interests. Declining a promotion that would make you miserable and ineffective is a sign of self-awareness, not lack of ambition. Propose an alternative growth path instead.
